subtype: Sadness after a loss in children [Actor]
passage: Two days after Dadi's funeral, Ritu sat by the buffalo shed and cried into her frock until her nose ran. An hour later she was hopping across chalk squares in the lane with Ayesha from next door, shrieking with laughter when Ayesha wobbled. At dusk, while Papa lit the lamp, Ritu asked, "When is Dadi coming back from the hospital?" It was the third time that day. Papa put the matchbox down. "Dadi died, Ritu. Her body stopped working, and she can't come back. We all miss her." Ritu nodded. Then she asked if she could still feed the buffalo in the morning, the way Dadi used to. "Yes," said Papa. "Six o'clock, same as always."

qa.q: What did Ritu ask Papa at dusk?
qa.a: When is Dadi coming back from the hospital?

qa.q: Why might Ritu keep asking the same question about Dadi?
qa.a: She is confused and still hoping; the idea that Dadi can never come back is hard for her to hold, so she checks again.

qa.q: What choice did Papa make when Ritu asked a third time, and why did it help?
qa.a: He stopped, gave the same honest, simple answer and kept the six o'clock routine, giving her both the truth and something steady.

qa.q: What might Ayesha think when Ritu laughs so soon after the funeral?
qa.a: Ayesha might be surprised, but Ritu's laughter is part of grief coming and going, not a sign that she has stopped missing Dadi.

grounding: It shows a village child grieving her Dadi by crying, playing happily and asking the same question again, helped by honest words and routine.

subtype: Sadness after a loss in children [Actor]
passage: On Sunday mornings in Toronto, Rania used to video-call Jiddo while Mum made pancakes. This Sunday the laptop stayed shut. Rania ate two pancakes, built a blanket fort with her little brother and laughed so hard she snorted. Then she saw Jiddo's old scarf on the hook and sobbed on the hallway floor. Her mother, Fatima, sat down beside her. After a while Rania whispered, "Did Jiddo die because I didn't call last week?" "No, habibti. Jiddo was very old and very sick. Nothing you did or didn't do made him die." At bedtime Rania asked again. Fatima gave the same answer, in the same gentle words. "Can we still have pancakes on Sundays?" "Every Sunday."

qa.q: What did Rania see that made her sob?
qa.a: Jiddo's old scarf on the hook.

qa.q: What was Rania worried about when she whispered to her mother?
qa.a: She was afraid that Jiddo died because she didn't call last week, so she felt it might be her fault.

qa.q: Which choice by Fatima at bedtime helped Rania, and why?
qa.a: Fatima answered the repeated question again with the same simple, honest words, without impatience, so Rania heard clearly that it was not her fault.

qa.q: How might Rania's little brother see her laughing in the fort and then crying soon after?
qa.a: He may be puzzled, but it shows that a grieving child can play happily one moment and cry the next; both are normal.

grounding: It shows a child abroad grieving Jiddo in waves of play and tears, repeating a question and needing honest words and the Sunday routine.

passage:
"Ma, when is Dadu coming back from the hospital?"
Gargi put down the spoon and sat beside her daughter. "Bidisha, Dadu died on Tuesday. His body stopped working. He can't come back."
Bidisha's face crumpled. She cried into her mother's sari for a long time.
Twenty minutes later she was on the floor with her cousin, laughing over ludo. "I got a six!"
At bedtime, after her bath and story, she asked again. "Ma, is Dadu still in the hospital?"
Gargi stroked her hair. "No, shona. Dadu died. We can't see him any more, but we can remember him."
"Can we look at his photo?"
"Yes. Let's look at it together."

qa.q: When did Dadu die?
qa.a: He died on Tuesday.

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel after hearing that Dadu died, and later?
qa.a: She felt very sad and cried hard, then later felt happy playing ludo, then sad again at bedtime.

qa.q: What did Gargi do that helps a grieving child?
qa.a: She used honest, simple words each time Bidisha asked, kept the bath and story routine and offered to look at Dadu's photo together.

qa.q: What might it be like for Gargi to answer the same question again?
qa.a: It may be painful and tiring for her, but she stays patient because she understands grief comes in waves for a child.

grounding: Shows a child grieving a grandparent who cries, plays happily, then asks the same question again, with a parent giving honest simple words and routine.

subtype: Sadness after a loss in children [Actor]
passage: When Nani died last winter, I was ten, and I didn't understand. I'm Ujjwal. Santosh Mama sat with me on the steps and said, "Nani's heart stopped. She died. She won't come back, and it's okay to feel very sad." I cried a lot. But the next day I played cricket with my cousins and laughed, and then I felt terrible, like I'd forgotten her. I asked Mama, "Is it bad that I laughed?" He said, "No. Sad and happy can take turns." We kept doing homework after school, like always. For weeks I kept asking where Nani was now. Mama always answered the same way, calmly. It still comes in waves. It's not my fault.

qa.q: What game did Ujjwal play the day after Nani died?
qa.a: Ujjwal played cricket with the cousins.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel after laughing at cricket?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt terrible and guilty, worried that laughing meant forgetting Nani.

qa.q: What helped Ujjwal cope with grief?
qa.a: Santosh Mama's honest, simple words, calm answers to repeated questions and keeping the usual homework routine.

qa.q: How might Santosh Mama have felt answering the same question for weeks?
qa.a: He may have felt sad himself, but he stayed calm and patient to help Ujjwal feel safe.

grounding: Shows a child grieving a grandparent who cries, laughs, then feels guilty and asks the same question again, supported by honest words and routine.

subtype: Sadness after a loss in children [Actor]
passage: Class note, Year 2, Thursday. Madhuri's Ammamma died last week. At circle time today she cried when we sang the morning song her Ammamma used to hum. At break she played happily with the skipping rope and laughed loudly. After lunch she asked me, "Can Ammamma see me from the sky?" She asked three times. Each time I gave the same honest, simple answer: "Ammamma has died. I don't know about the sky, but you can remember her and talk about her anytime." I kept our class routine the same. I told her mother at pickup, who said Madhuri asks at home too. We agreed this is normal for her age. Next: a memory drawing next week, if she wants. — Rajni

qa.q: How many times did Madhuri ask about Ammamma?
qa.a: She asked three times.

qa.q: What did Madhuri feel when the class sang the morning song?
qa.a: She felt sad and grieving, crying because Ammamma used to hum that song.

qa.q: What did Rajni do that helps a child through grief?
qa.a: Rajni gave the same honest, simple answer each time, kept the class routine steady and talked with Madhuri's mother.

qa.q: How might Madhuri's mother feel hearing from Rajni?
qa.a: She may feel reassured that Madhuri's repeated questions and changing moods are normal and that school is supporting her.

grounding: Shows a child grieving a grandparent in waves, crying then playing then asking again, with a teacher giving honest simple words and routine.

subtype: Sadness after a loss in children [Actor]
passage:
Saturday
Dadaji died on Tuesday. Today I cried in the morning when I saw his glasses on the shelf. Mummy hugged me for a long time.
Then Joseph from next door came over and we played cricket in the lane. I hit a six over the gate and laughed so much. Then I felt bad for laughing.
At dinner I asked Mummy again, "Is Dadaji really never coming back?" I already asked yesterday. She didn't get cross. She said, "No, beta. His body stopped working. He can't come back. But we can talk about him whenever you want."
She said it's okay to be sad and okay to laugh. Tomorrow is school, like normal. I'm going to keep his glasses in my drawer.
Yogesh

qa.q: What did Yogesh see on the shelf that caused tears?
qa.a: Dadaji's glasses on the shelf.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel after laughing during cricket?
qa.a: Yogesh felt guilty for laughing, even though the game had been fun, because Dadaji had just died.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that could help any grieving child?
qa.a: She answered the repeated question honestly and simply without getting cross, said both sadness and laughter are okay, and kept the normal routine.

qa.q: What is it like for Mummy when Yogesh asks the same question again?
qa.a: She is likely grieving too and finds it painful, but she stays patient and gentle.

grounding: Yogesh cries, plays happily and asks the same question again after Dadaji's death, and Mummy gives honest, simple words and routine.
